blocks.text: Chapter 1.
Preacher, Prosecutor, Politician — or Scientist?
A new fire tonight, friend — and it begins inside a wall of flame, racing up a Montana hillside at seven hundred feet per minute.

August 1949. Fifteen smokejumpers parachute into Mann Gulch expecting a routine fire. The wind shifts. The blaze leaps the gulch. And suddenly the crew is sprinting uphill for their lives, flames closing behind them faster than any man can run — with the safety of the ridge just a few hundred yards away.
Twelve of the fifteen will die on that slope. And the two details of how they died — and how one man lived — hold the entire lesson of Adam Grant's book.
The man who lit a fire to survive one

Foreman Wagner Dodge survived through one of the most stunning acts of rethinking ever recorded. Racing the flames, he suddenly stopped running — struck a match — and set fire to the grass ahead of him. An escape fire: by burning the fuel around him and lying down in the fresh ashes, he made a hole in the fire's food supply, and the wall of flame roared past him. He invented the technique on the spot, in seconds, mid-sprint. None of his crew joined him — the idea was too foreign, and there was no time to explain.

Pause and guess: The subtler tragedy came out in the investigations afterward. The men who died were carrying something as they ran — and analyses suggested some could have outrun the fire without it. What were they carrying, and why didn't they drop it?
Ready? Here is what happened.

Their tools. Axes, saws, heavy packs — the men died running uphill with equipment they never dropped, and the same thing happened again in 1994 on Storm King Mountain, where firefighters died still wearing packs and clutching their tools. Why not drop them? Because carrying equipment is what firefighters do, friend — abandoning the tools felt like abandoning who they were. And that is Grant's opening thunderclap: we all run with our tools. Our tools are the assumptions, habits, and beliefs that once served us — and the more they've defined our success and identity, the harder they are to release, even when they're the very weight slowing us down. In a world obsessed with learning, the most neglected skill is unlearning: knowing when to let a hard-won belief go. Sometimes it's an intellectual nicety. Sometimes — as on that hillside — it's survival.
The four hats
Why don't we rethink? Because when we think and talk, Grant says — building on Tetlock's work — we slip into three professional costumes, and none of them involves changing our own mind.

Preacher mode: our sacred beliefs feel threatened, so we sermonize — the goal is conversion, not truth. Prosecutor mode: we spot the flaws in other people's reasoning and marshal the case to convict them — winning replaces learning. Politician mode: we campaign for an audience's approval — lobbying, flattering, telling constituents what they want — updating what we say without ever updating what we think. In all three modes, friend, being right is a foregone conclusion; the only live question is how to defend, attack, or sell.

The fourth hat is thinking like a scientist — no lab coat required. It's a mindset: humility over pride, doubt over certainty, curiosity over closure. Your opinions become hypotheses; your decisions become experiments; disagreements become chances to learn rather than battles to win. And Grant is careful with the sting in the tail: actual scientists aren't immune — defending pet theories, credentialed researchers preach, prosecute, and politick like anyone. Scientist mode is a discipline anyone can practice... and any scientist can abandon. As Grant puts it: if knowledge is power, knowing what you don't know is wisdom.
The Italian experiment

Does the fourth hat actually pay — or does it just make for nicer conversations? Economist Arnaldo Camuffo ran the test as a genuine randomized trial: over a hundred founders of early-stage Italian startups — furniture, food, healthcare, retail — all given the same four-month entrepreneurship course. The treatment group got one addition: they were taught to think like scientists — strategy as theory, customer interviews as hypothesis development, product launches as experiments whose results dictate persist, adjust, or pivot.
Pause and guess: One year later, the control-group startups averaged under $300 in revenue. What did the scientist-trained founders average — and what did they do more than twice as often?
Ready? Here is what happened.

Over $12,000 — roughly forty times more — earned more than twice as fast. And they pivoted more than twice as often. Watch the mechanism, friend: control-group founders preached the virtues of their original idea, prosecuted the critics who doubted it, and politicked by hyping it — anchored to plan A because admitting fault felt like failure. The scientist-founders changed course freely, because to a scientist a rejected hypothesis is just information. Grant draws the two trajectories as opposing loops. The overconfidence cycle: pride → conviction → confirmation bias (seeing what you expect) and desirability bias (seeing what you want) → validation → more pride. The rethinking cycle: humility → doubt → curiosity → discovery → new learning → honest humility again. The first loop feels wonderful and calcifies. The second feels uncomfortable... and compounds.
The genius who wouldn't drop his keyboard

Mike Lazaridis was a true prodigy — electronics-obsessed from childhood, co-founder of Research In Motion, creator of the BlackBerry: the device that brilliantly reimagined the phone as a secure wireless email machine with a beloved physical keyboard. By mid-2009, BlackBerry held nearly half the US smartphone market.
By 2014: less than 1 percent.

Not a failure of intelligence, friend — a failure of rethinking. When the iPhone arrived, Lazaridis dismissed the ideas at its heart: he couldn't accept that people would want a whole computer in their pocket rather than a focused email device; that they'd tolerate typing on glass instead of his keyboard; that home users choosing apps would outweigh IT departments choosing security. Years into the collapse, engineers' proposals kept being rebuffed for clashing with his original theory of what a smartphone was. His past success became proof, in his own mind, that his assumptions were permanent truths — the vision that built the company became the tool he wouldn't drop. And intelligence makes this trap worse, not better: research shows the smarter people are, the better they argue their own side — strong quantitative reasoners are more polarized on charged questions, using their skill to twist the data home. Add the "I'm not biased" bias — the near-universal certainty that bias afflicts everyone but us — and the fortress is complete.
The eraser studies

Why is rethinking so rare? Partly because we are cognitive misers — clinging to old views is cheap, wrestling with new ones is costly — and partly because doubt destabilizes identity, so we seize and freeze: grab an answer that gives closure and lock it in. We even romanticize the laziness as wisdom: generations of students have been told never to second-guess themselves on tests. Always trust your first instinct.

Psychologist Justin Kruger tested the folklore directly — by counting eraser marks on more than 1,500 students' exams. Only about a quarter of answer changes went right-to-wrong. Half went wrong-to-right. And a review of 33 studies on answer changing found that in every single one, the majority of revisions improved scores. The first-instinct fallacy is exactly backwards, friend: changing answers doesn't hurt on average — hesitating to reconsider does. And it extends far past exams: we cling to first impressions of people, stale career plans, and outdated mental models exactly the way we cling to answer A. Grant's homely prescription: treat your beliefs like possessions at spring cleaning — schedule a recurring belief checkup, pick one conviction formed years ago, and ask whether it deserves re-examination against everything you know now. This week: rewrite one strong opinion as a hypothesis, state what evidence would change your mind... and go look for that evidence.
Before you go

So: twelve men died running with tools they should have dropped, and one lived by lighting a fire nobody understood; three costumes — preacher, prosecutor, politician — guarantee you never change your mind, while the scientist's hat made Italian founders forty times richer; the smartest defender falls hardest; and the eraser studies prove your first instinct was never sacred. The enemy, Grant says, is not ignorance. It is the illusion that what you already know is enough.

But a puzzle remains for tomorrow, friend. If doubt is so valuable... how much doubt? Surely there's a valley between crippling insecurity and blind arrogance — and it turns out that valley has a map, drawn from the strangest of sources: a mountain everyone climbs with confidence they haven't earned. Next time: the sweet spot of confidence — armchair quarterbacks, impostors, and the peak of Mount Stupid.
Key takeaways
We all run with our tools: the beliefs behind past success are the hardest — and sometimes most vital — to drop.
Three modes block rethinking (preach, prosecute, politick); scientist mode treats opinions as hypotheses and decisions as experiments.
The Italian RCT: scientist-trained founders earned ~40x the revenue and pivoted twice as often — a rejected hypothesis is just information.
BlackBerry fell from ~50% to <1%: intelligence sharpens the defense of stale assumptions rather than dissolving them.
The first-instinct fallacy is backwards: across 33 studies, most answer changes go wrong-to-right — hesitating to reconsider is the real cost.
Schedule belief checkups: rewrite one conviction as a hypothesis, name the evidence that would change your mind, and hunt for it.
